tier_reason: BENCHMARKS.md states the compiler (Clang 17.0.3, MSVC-like command line), the build (release with default compiler flags, i.e. the CMake Release defaults) and the CPU (AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, Windows 10). The benchmark code is public in src/benchmark (main.cpp, triangulator_benchmark.cpp, impl/detria.cpp, impl/cdt.cpp, impl/poly2tri.cpp, impl/triangle.cpp). src/benchmark/CMakeLists.txt pins CDT and poly2tri by git commit, and Triangle is vendored in src/benchmark/3rdParty/triangle.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Medians from the 23 per-case SVG result files embedded in BENCHMARKS.md (images/benchmark/*.svg), detria vs CDT vs Triangle in ms: world land outline (407,072 vertices) 502 vs 1431 vs 441; United States outline 24.4 vs 58.8 vs 27.2; Afghanistan (1,532 vertices) 0.74 vs 2.17 vs 0.87; 10,000-vertex debug2.dat 11.6 vs 28.7 vs 12.5. Over the 23 files, detria is faster than CDT in 21 (about 1.5x to 3.2x, derived from page data) and faster than poly2tri in all 14 cases poly2tri supports (about 1.05x to 2.2x, derived from page data). It is faster than Triangle in 16 of 23: the 13 country outlines, city.dat, debug2.dat and the depth-4 fractal (1.66 vs 1.73 ms), by about 1.04x to 1.3x (derived from page data). It is slower than Triangle on all four random-point sets (1,000,000 points: 1798 vs 946 ms) and on the world land outline (502 vs 441 ms). It is slower than both Triangle and CDT on the depth-6 and depth-8 cocircular fractals (depth 8: 3091 vs 1407 CDT vs 857 Triangle).
corrections.caveats: Mixed result. The library beats CDT and poly2tri on most inputs. Against Triangle it wins only by 4-30% on country outlines, poly2tri test files and the small fractal, and it loses on random points (up to about 1.9x slower at 1M points), the world land outline and the deeper fractals (3.6x slower than Triangle at depth 8). 'Default compiler flags' means the CMake Release defaults for clang-cl, not explicit flags. Baseline versions are pinned in src/benchmark/CMakeLists.txt (CDT 58f34da, poly2tri 13d64e7, Triangle vendored), but no release numbers are given. The machine is a single 2019 Windows desktop. Neither CDT nor poly2tri is the category's incumbent, and CGAL, Boost.Geometry and GEOS are not compared. Triangle's own license is non-commercial; detria is MIT or WTFPL, so this does not affect detria. The benchmark images date from 2024 (last benchmark-image commit 2024-05-03), and later commits changed the code.

notes: I parsed all 23 SVG result files from raw.githubusercontent.com and re-tallied the medians. Every number in the record matches. The only error was the list of Triangle wins, which left out the depth-4 fractal. License, stars (13), last commit (2025-03-02) and stale status all check out.

tier_reason: docs/benchmarks.md gives the compiler and flags (Apple clang 17, -std=c++17 -O2 -DNDEBUG, Release), the CPU (Apple M1) and library versions (Boost 1.90.0, s2geometry 0.14.0, GeographicLib 2.7). The Google Benchmark code is public under benchmarks/ (bench_geo_utils, bench_boost, bench_s2, bench_geographiclib, with shared inputs from benchmarks/common/random_data.hpp).

corrections.claimed_speedup: contains (M queries/s, geo-utils-cpp vs Boost.Geometry): 16.2 vs 1.91 at N=10, 2.87 vs 0.234 at N=100, 0.329 vs 0.024 at N=1000 (about 8.5x, 12x and 14x, derived from page data). area (M polygons/s): 69.9 vs 45.0 at N=10, 67.2 vs 36.2 at N=100, 67.7 vs 36.6 at N=1000 (about 1.5-1.9x, derived from page data). heading is about 1.05-1.1x faster (24.9 vs 22.5 at N=1000, 15.5 vs 14.7 at N=100,000). distance_between (40.5 vs 39.8 and 28.2 vs 28.8) and path_length (54.0 vs 48.7 down to 41.7 vs 40.2) tie Boost.Geometry within noise.
corrections.caveats: The contains comparison is not like for like. geo-utils-cpp uses an O(N) ray cast over rhumb-line edges by default, while bg::within with the spherical CS picks a great-circle winding strategy. So the two give different answers near the poles and on long edges, and the 8-14x gap partly reflects that choice (the docs say so). S2 beats it by a wide margin on contains (18.0 M/s at N=100), on path_length (about 2x) and on snap-to-route (about 3x). The benchmarks were run on one machine only (Apple M1, Apple clang), with no GCC, MSVC or x86 numbers. The library is a C++ port of the geometry utilities in Google's android-maps-utils (Java, Apache-2.0). The repo is young: the oldest visible commit is from May 2026.

notes: Every number in the record appears in docs/benchmarks.md. I added the small heading win and the path_length tie, and the caveat that the library is a port of android-maps-utils (Java, so this is not a duplicate of a C++ entry). Apache-2.0, 56 stars, last commit 2026-09-20 and not a fork all confirmed.

tier_reason: The README table compares kigumi against CGAL corefinement and states the compiler (Homebrew Clang 22.1.1) and the CPU (MacBook Pro 14-inch M4, 16-core). The benchmark code is public: benches/kigumi/main.cc and benches/corefinement/main.cc both use the EPECK kernel and time only the Boolean call, tools/run_benches.sh and tools/gen_bench_meshes.sh drive them, and the input meshes are in meshes/. The documented ./run configure pins -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, which is the same standard as the ryu and fast_double_parser A precedents.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Homebrew Clang 22.1.1; CMake Release via ./run configure (-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, so CMake's default -O3 -DNDEBUG; benches/*/CMakeLists.txt add only warning flags); benches need -DKIGUMI_BUILD_BENCHES=ON; CGAL and the other dependencies are pinned by the vcpkg submodule (b42535f)
corrections.caveats: The README states neither mesh sizes nor library versions, although the input meshes are in meshes/ and the CGAL and libigl versions are pinned by the vcpkg submodule. The README's build steps do not show the -DKIGUMI_BUILD_BENCHES=ON switch the benchmarks need. The 'Open' sequential gain over CGAL is only 1.3x. Manifold beats kigumi on closed meshes but is approximate, and geogram (5.5 s) is the only other tool that handles the open-and-closed case. A '16-core CPU' in a 14-inch M4 MacBook Pro means the M4 Max, not the base M4. The benchmarks ran on a single machine, and the table predates the 2026-07-20 'Autorefinement' change (the last 'Update benchmarks' commit is from 2026-03-19). kigumi's own code is MIT, but it needs CGAL's kernel (LGPL) and 2D Triangulations (GPL or commercial), so a binary that uses it carries GPL obligations unless CGAL is licensed commercially.

notes: All README numbers match. I changed usability from mixed to copyable because every part is under an OSI license (MIT code, with LGPL/GPL CGAL dependencies) and nothing is unlicensed; the GPL obligation is in caveats. MIT, 54 stars, last commit 2026-08-31 and not a fork all confirmed.
